title: The rich man and Lazarus (Luke 16:19–31)
hookLine: a beggar at the gate has a name; the rich man doesn't

cards: The man who sells the newspaper. The woman who cleans the office after everyone goes home. Someone by the same doorway each morning with a paper cup.
Faces seen every day, with no names. Jesus tells a story about a gate and two men on either side of it. Only one gets a name, and it isn't the one you'd expect.
Some readers point out that no other character in his parables is named at all.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "There was a certain rich man, which was clothed in purple and fine linen, and fared sumptuously every day." Purple was the cloth of kings.

"And there was a certain beggar named Lazarus, which was laid at his gate, full of sores." Laid there, as if someone carried him. He longs for crumbs from the table, and the dogs come and lick his sores.
Lazarus is a Greek form of the Hebrew name Eleazar, usually explained as God has helped. Nobody else is helping him.
The rich man has no name at all; later tradition called him Dives, but that's just the Latin word for rich. Both men die. Lazarus is carried by angels to Abraham's side; the rich man is in torment.
And here's the detail that stings. The rich man calls across: send Lazarus to cool my tongue.

teach.h: THE GULF BEGAN AT THE GATE.
teach.b: Every time he passed that gate, he knew who was lying there. The story never says he kicked or cursed him. He just didn't see him as someone his to help.
Abraham answers that a great gulf is now fixed between them.
The rich man begs for Lazarus to warn his five brothers. They have Moses and the prophets, Abraham says, and "neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead."
Christians differ on how literally to read the afterlife scenes; some take them as a parable, not a map. Either way, the story starts at the gate. The gulf began there.

how: Christians read this parable when thinking about wealth and about those at their own gate, and some church outreach to people living on the street begins with learning names.

o: the angel who carried a beggar to Abraham's side
the rich man in purple, later called Dives
the beggar at the gate; the name means God has helped

games.q: what's inside Luke 16:19–31 — tap the pairs.

s: the Bible names the rich man Dives
Luke gives him no name. Dives is just the Latin word for rich, used by later tradition.
Abraham says the five brothers already have Moses and the prophets
"they have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them."
the rich man didn't know who Lazarus was
in the story he asks for Lazarus by name. he knew him all along.

games.q: the rich man, in torment, begs Abraham to send Lazarus to warn his five brothers. what does Abraham say?
o: yes, Lazarus will go at once.
they have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them.
games.why: "they have Moses and the prophets." and if they won't hear them, "neither will they be persuaded, though one rose from the dead."

practice: Picture your ordinary route through a day, the street, the shop, the bus, and let the faces you pass again and again come up one by one: the cleaner, the guard, the cashier with the tired smile. Notice whose names you don't know.
If you pray, hold each of them before God, even without a name.

wordCard.voice: Lazarus, a Greek form of Eleazar, God has helped: the beggar at the gate, whose name the rich man knew all along.

orig.note: Hebrew: Eleazar, God has helped. Lazarus is its Greek form.

carryVoice: Your line: the beggar had a name. Every face at the gate has one. Day five hundred sixty-one.
